questions.q: Ordinary least squares minimises what?
options: The sum of squared residuals $\sum_i(y_i - x_i^\top w)^2$
questions.why: Squared error gives a closed-form solution through the normal equations and corresponds to maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.

questions.q: Why is the intercept usually left out of the ridge penalty?
options: Penalising it would make predictions depend on where the target's origin is
questions.why: Shifting $y$ by a constant should shift the intercept, not change the slopes. Centring the data and fitting the intercept separately achieves this.

questions.q: Why does the lasso produce exactly-zero coefficients but ridge doesn't?
options: The L1 penalty's corners let the optimum sit on an axis; the L2 penalty's gradient vanishes at zero
questions.why: In coordinate descent the lasso update is a soft-threshold, which sets a coefficient to 0 whenever its correlation with the residual is below $\lambda$.

questions.q: Logistic regression's decision boundary is...
options: A sigmoid curve in feature space
Linear in the features: the set where $w^\top x + b = 0$
questions.why: The sigmoid maps the linear score to a probability, but the threshold $p = 0.5$ corresponds to a hyperplane.

questions.q: On perfectly linearly separable data, unregularised logistic regression's weights do what?
options: Grow without bound, because scaling them up always lowers the loss
Converge to a unique finite value
questions.why: The likelihood keeps improving as predictions approach 0 and 1. A small L2 penalty keeps the solution finite.

questions.q: Softmax regression with $K$ classes has how many independent sets of weights?
options: $K - 1$, since adding the same vector to every class leaves the probabilities unchanged
questions.why: The softmax is invariant to a shared shift. In practice all $K$ are kept and regularisation picks a unique solution.

questions.q: Two features are almost perfectly correlated. What happens to OLS coefficients?
options: They become unstable with large variance, although predictions may stay fine
One is always set to zero
questions.why: $X^\top X$ is near singular, so small data changes swing the coefficients. Ridge stabilises them.

questions.q: Which assumption does the OLS standard error formula rely on?
options: Errors with constant variance (homoscedasticity) and no correlation
questions.why: With heteroscedastic or correlated errors the estimates are still unbiased, but the usual standard errors are wrong; robust errors fix that.

questions.q: k-NN with $k = 1$ has what training error?
options: Zero (barring duplicate points with different labels)
The same as the test error
questions.why: Each training point is its own nearest neighbour. That is why training error is useless for picking $k$.

questions.q: Why must features be scaled before k-NN?
options: Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges
It makes the algorithm faster only
questions.why: A feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in fractions. Standardising gives each feature comparable influence.

questions.q: Gaussian naive Bayes assumes what?
options: Features are jointly Gaussian with a full covariance
Features are conditionally independent given the class, each Gaussian
Features are independent of the class
questions.why: The independence assumption makes the likelihood a product of 1-D Gaussians. It is rarely true, but rankings are often still good.

questions.q: In naive Bayes, why compute the log of the posterior instead of the product?
options: Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to zero
Logs make it linear in the classes
Logs are required by Bayes' rule
questions.why: Summing log-likelihoods keeps numbers in range; the argmax is unchanged.

questions.q: The perceptron is guaranteed to converge when...
options: The learning rate is small enough
There are more features than samples
questions.why: On non-separable data it cycles forever. The averaged perceptron gives a more stable answer in that case.

questions.q: LDA differs from QDA how?
options: LDA assumes all classes share one covariance, giving linear boundaries
questions.why: With a shared covariance the quadratic terms cancel. QDA's per-class covariances give quadratic boundaries but need more data.

questions.q: A linear SVM's hinge loss $\max(0, 1 - y\,w^\top x)$ is zero for which points?
options: Correctly classified points with margin at least 1
questions.why: Points beyond the margin contribute nothing, so the solution depends only on points on or inside the margin: the support vectors.

questions.q: The SVM regularisation parameter $C$ is large. What does that do?
options: Penalises margin violations heavily, giving a narrower margin and less regularisation
questions.why: Large $C$ trusts the training data more and risks overfitting; small $C$ allows more violations for a wider margin.

questions.q: The Gini impurity of a node with class proportions $0.5, 0.5$ is...
questions.why: $1 - \sum p_k^2 = 1 - 0.25 - 0.25$. A pure node has impurity 0.

questions.q: Why do decision trees not need feature scaling?
options: Splits depend only on the ordering of values within a feature
questions.why: Any monotone transformation of a feature gives the same splits.

questions.q: Bagging reduces which part of the error most?
questions.why: Averaging many models trained on bootstrap samples smooths out their individual fluctuations; it does little for a model that is systematically wrong.

questions.q: How does a random forest decorrelate its trees beyond bagging?
options: It prunes every tree to depth 1
It uses a different loss per tree
Each split considers only a random subset of features
questions.why: Without feature subsampling, one strong feature would dominate the top split of every tree, making them similar.

questions.q: AdaBoost reweights training examples after each round. Which examples gain weight?
options: The ones with the largest features
Those the current weak learner misclassified
questions.why: Increasing the weight on mistakes forces the next learner to focus on them; each learner's vote is weighted by its accuracy.

questions.q: Gradient boosting for squared loss fits each new tree to what?
options: The residuals of the current ensemble
questions.why: Residuals are the negative gradient of squared error. For other losses the tree fits the corresponding negative gradient.

questions.q: Why use a small learning rate (shrinkage) in gradient boosting?
options: Smaller steps with more trees usually generalise better
questions.why: Shrinkage is a form of regularisation; the cost is needing more boosting rounds.

questions.q: Stacking should train the meta-model on which predictions?
options: The base models' predictions on their own training data
Out-of-fold predictions from the base models
questions.why: In-sample predictions are overconfident, so the meta-model would learn to trust the base models too much.

questions.q: Permutation importance measures a feature's importance by...
options: How much the validation score drops when that feature's values are shuffled
The number of splits using it
questions.why: Shuffling breaks the feature's link to the target while keeping its distribution. Correlated features can share importance, making each look less important.

questions.q: k-means minimises what objective?
options: The maximum distance within a cluster
The sum of squared distances from points to their assigned centroid
questions.why: Alternating assignment and centroid updates never increases this objective, so the algorithm converges, although only to a local optimum.

questions.q: Why does k-means++ seeding help?
options: It chooses the optimal number of clusters
It spreads initial centroids out, picking points with probability proportional to squared distance from existing centroids
questions.why: Better starting points reduce bad local optima and come with an $O(\log k)$ approximation guarantee in expectation.

questions.q: DBSCAN labels a point as noise when...
options: It is neither a core point nor within `eps` of a core point
It is the last point visited
Its cluster has fewer than $k$ points
It is far from the centroid
questions.why: Core points have at least `min_samples` neighbours within `eps`. DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape and doesn't need $k$.

questions.q: Single-linkage agglomerative clustering tends to produce what?
options: Long chain-like clusters, because merges use the closest pair of points
questions.why: Single linkage joins clusters through any nearby pair; complete and average linkage favour compact groups.

questions.q: A Gaussian mixture fitted with EM differs from k-means how?
options: It makes soft assignments and models each cluster's covariance
It always finds the global optimum
questions.why: k-means is a limit of a GMM with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments.

questions.q: The E-step of EM for a GMM computes...
options: Each point's responsibility (posterior probability) for each component
questions.why: The M-step then re-estimates weights, means and covariances using those responsibilities.

questions.q: Isolation forest scores a point as anomalous when...
options: It is close to many points
Random splits isolate it in few steps (short average path length)
It has a long path length
questions.why: Anomalies are few and different, so random partitions separate them quickly.

questions.q: In t-SNE, what does perplexity control?
options: The effective number of neighbours each point considers
questions.why: A per-point Gaussian bandwidth is found by binary search so that the conditional distribution's perplexity matches the target value.

questions.q: Why stratify k-fold splits for classification?
options: To ensure each fold has one class
To keep class proportions similar in every fold
questions.why: With rare classes, unstratified folds can miss a class entirely, making scores noisy.

questions.q: For time series, why not use random k-fold?
options: Time series have too few points
Training on the future to predict the past leaks information
questions.why: Use forward-chaining splits where each validation fold comes after its training data.

questions.q: Log loss heavily penalises which predictions?
options: Confident wrong predictions, such as $p = 0.99$ for a negative
questions.why: $-\log(1 - 0.99) \approx 4.6$. A single prediction of exactly 0 or 1 that is wrong makes the loss infinite, so implementations clip.

questions.q: ROC AUC is insensitive to what?
options: Any monotone transformation of the scores
questions.why: AUC depends only on the ranking. That is also why it says nothing about calibration.

questions.q: With 1% positives, why can precision-recall be more informative than ROC?
options: ROC can't be computed with imbalance
ROC's false-positive rate stays small even with many false positives, while precision reveals them
questions.why: With 99,000 negatives, 1,000 false positives is only a 1% FPR but can halve precision.

questions.q: Average precision summarises what?
options: The precision-recall curve, as precision averaged over the recall levels of each positive
questions.why: It weights precision at each threshold by the increase in recall, giving a single number for ranking quality on positives.

questions.q: Mean absolute error versus RMSE: which penalises large errors more?
questions.why: Squaring emphasises large errors. MAE is more robust to outliers and is minimised by the median rather than the mean.

questions.q: You pick hyperparameters by cross-validation and report that CV score as your final performance. What is the problem?
options: Cross-validation can't be used for selection
The score is optimistically biased because it was used for selection; report a held-out test score
questions.why: Selecting the best of many configurations on the same folds overfits to them. Nested CV or a separate test set gives an unbiased estimate.

questions.q: Imputing missing values with the column mean should use which mean?
options: The overall mean of all splits
The training set's, applied to validation and test
questions.why: Using statistics from evaluation data leaks information. Fit the imputer on training data only.

questions.q: One-hot encoding a category seen only at test time should produce what?
options: An all-zero vector (or an explicit "unknown" column)
A copy of the most common category
questions.why: The encoder must handle unseen values gracefully. Grouping rare categories into "other" also helps.

questions.q: Which scaler is most robust to outliers?
options: Robust scaling with the median and interquartile range
questions.why: The median and IQR barely move when a few extreme values are added, unlike the min, max, mean and standard deviation.

questions.q: For a linear model, why drop one column of a one-hot encoding when an intercept is present?
options: One-hot encodings can't be used with intercepts
The columns sum to 1, which is collinear with the intercept
questions.why: With all columns and an intercept, $X^\top X$ is singular. Regularised models tolerate keeping all columns.

questions.q: Label-encoding a nominal feature (red = 0, green = 1, blue = 2) for a linear model introduces what problem?
options: A false ordering and spacing between categories
questions.why: The model would treat blue as "twice green". Trees are less affected because they can split anywhere.

questions.q: A pairwise distance matrix for $n = 100{,}000$ points in float64 needs about how much memory?
questions.why: $10^{10}$ entries times 8 bytes. Large-scale neighbour search uses approximate indexes instead.

questions.q: Target encoding (replacing a category with the mean target) risks what if done naively?
options: Leakage: each row's own target influences its feature
questions.why: Compute the encoding out of fold (or with smoothing) so a row's label doesn't feed its own feature.

questions.q: Log-transforming a right-skewed positive feature helps a linear model because...
options: It makes the feature normally distributed in every case
It compresses large values, making relationships closer to linear and reducing the influence of extremes
It is required for gradient descent
questions.why: Many multiplicative effects become additive in log space. Use `log1p` when zeros are possible.
